text:
Counting words. Guessing the next word from the last one. Giving rare words extra weight. These ideas are much older than they look. The youngest of the three is over fifty. The oldest is nearly a hundred. So here's how the field got here, oldest first.

It starts in the nineteen thirties, when the linguist George Zipf counted words. Rank them by how common they are, and the counts fall off roughly as one over the rank. That's Zipf's law. Here's the course's count of Jane Austen's Emma. The top is rough: the first two words almost tie. But a hundred words make up sixty percent of the book, and of its seven thousand different words, nearly four in ten appear just once. Next, counts like these became a way to predict.

In nineteen forty-eight, Claude Shannon founded information theory. Tucked inside his paper: guess the next word from the one before, by how often each word follows another. He even made text that way, by hand: open a book at random, find the word, copy the one after it, repeat. Here's what came out. The head and in frontal attack on an English writer... It reads like English, and says nothing. The course's tiny version does the same: after the word the, cat comes three times and dog twice, so it guesses cat. That's an n-gram model. Today's language models still make that guess, with far more than counts behind it. But could a machine that strings words together ever hold a conversation?
